title: Graceful Failback Lane and Tenant Hedge PRD - concept
content:
Executive summary:

This note proposes a paired feature set for Dedicated capacity customers: a Graceful Failback Lane (GFL) and Tenant Hedge Credits (THC). The GFL is an operational and API-level mechanism that allows tenant workloads to transparently fail over to a controlled fallback path (hosted/soft-degradation variants) with bounded impact to latency SLAs and billing behavior. The THC system provides a small time-decaying credit/insurance pool that tenants can opt into to smooth perceived disruptions and reduce noisy-eviction churn during demand spikes or transient capacity pressure. Together these primitives aim to: preserve customer availability, reduce support churn, and enable predictable economics for Reserved Dedicated pools during bursts or partial outages.

Problem statement:
- Dedicated pools face two recurring hard problems: (1) sudden transient demand surges that would either cause throttling/eviction or force expensive overprovisioning, and (2) cross-tenant noisy neighbors causing brittle degradation for a minority of tenants.
- Current strategies (hard preemption, coarse burst credits, total fallback to hosted) can be jarring for customers — lead to failed requests, large quality regressions, or surprising cost spikes.
- We need an approach that is: incremental, observable, tenant-configurable, and minimizes operator involvement.

Goals:
- Provide a controlled, reversible failback path for dedicated tenants that keeps critical requests live even when Dedicated capacity is constrained.
- Offer tenants a lightweight hedging mechanism (credits + policy) so they can opt to smooth their experience without committing to permanent higher-reserved capacity.
- Integrate with autoscaler and admission control so decisions are latency-SLO-aware and economically bounded.
- Surface telemetry and billing signals so customers and SRE can understand failback events and hedging consumption.

Non-goals:
- This is not a replacement for long-term capacity planning or a substitute for buying larger Reserved commitments.
- We will not initially support full stateful migration of KV caches or large model shards across environments; failback applies at request routing + model variant level.

Key concepts and primitives:
1) Graceful Failback Lane (GFL):
   - A routing policy layer that routes requests originally intended for Dedicated pool -> fallback path under defined triggers. Fallback path options: (A) hosted identical model (paid per-token), (B) lower-fidelity quantized model in Dedicated (same pool but different resource class), (C) regionally proximate Dedicated spare pool.
   - Trigger signals: pool saturation (CPU/GPU util percent + queue depth), explicit shard preemption events, and autoscaler decommit grace windows.
   - Failback windows: requests routed to fallback include metadata so downstream tracing, billing, and quality monitors can attribute them. Fallbacks are reversible per-request; subsequent requests attempt to return to dedicated lane when signals clear.

2) Tenant Hedge Credits (THC):
   - Each tenant can enroll to a small hedging account at purchase/renewal time (opt-in). The hedging account has: credit balance (token-equivalent), a time-decay policy (e.g., half-life 7 days), and a burn policy for different fallback types.
   - Credits pay for the incremental cost difference during failback (e.g., hosted per-token delta, or cost of higher-priority slots) so tenant experience is smoothed without sudden bill surprises.
   - If credits deplete, failback either becomes subject to tenant-level hard throttling, or customer receives a notification and a brief grace window.

3) Quiet-scale and Soft-Admission Controls:
   - Admission control is augmented with quiet-scale: when demand spikes, we prefer throttling for best-effort routes but quietly ramp failback for critical routes (tagged via traffic priorities). Quiet-scale reduces oscillations by staggering decisions across tenants and using exponential backoff for reattachment to Dedicated.

4) Contracted QoS Profiles:
   - Tenants can declare QoS tiers for routes: critical, best-effort, background. GFL/THC decisions respect these tiers and default to protecting critical routes first.

Architecture and flow (high level):
- On request: SDK/route metadata indicates tenant ID + route QoS. Admission layer checks Dedicated slot availability and SLO headroom. If headroom exists, route to Dedicated. If not, consult Hedging credit balance and tenant QoS:
  - If enrolled and credits available & route priority >= configured threshold -> route to Failback Lane variant (hosted/quantized) and debit credits proportionally.
  - If not enrolled or credits exhausted -> apply configured fallback (throttle, 503, or deny) per tenant policy.
- Every routed failback emits structured telemetry: failback_type, credit_delta, pool_signal_snapshot, model_variant_id, request_id.

APIs and customer controls (proposal):
- New customer-facing bools/configs in Dedicated tenancy settings: "enable_failback" (on/off), "failback_preference" ([hosted, quant, spare_pool]), "hedge_enrollment" (on/off), "hedge_auto_replenish" (monthly add-ons), "route_qos_defaults" (map).
- Admin API endpoints: GET /tenancies/{id}/hedge -> returns balance, decay window, consumption history; POST /tenancies/{id}/hedge/replenish -> add credits; GET /pools/{id}/failback-snapshot -> recent failbacks, top tenants, average latency delta.

Operational changes & telemetry:
- New metrics to surface: failback_rate_by_tenant, hedge_burn_rate, mean_latency_delta_on_failback, failback_recovery_time, admission_retries, quiet_scale_backoff_index.
- Console: per-route timeline of failback events, heatmap of tenants consuming hedges, and per-tenant cost delta estimates.
- Alerts: pool-level failback rate > X% triggers capacity ops; tenant-level excessive hedge spend triggers customer success outreach.

Autoscaler and policy integration:
- Autoscaler should be fed a failback-corrected utilization signal (i.e., increase in hosted usage due to failback should influence decisions to scale Dedicated up if within burst capacity policies).
- Soft decommit windows: when scaling down dedicated nodes, the system should attempt to gently shift load to failback lane before preemption; use hedges to reduce request failures during the window.

Billing and economics:
- Hedge credits priced as a predictable add-on (monthly blocks) with transparent usage logs.
- Failback routing that uses hosted models is billed normally; THC is billed automatically to absorb delta up to credit balance. Customers get monthly reports detailing hedge usage and cost avoided (estimated).

Runbooks and SRE playbook excerpts:
- Detection: alert on sustained pool failback rate > 5% for 10m.
- Mitigation: temporarily expand burst pool (if capacity available), enable emergency reclamation of idle jobs, or toggle tenant-level failback-preference to spare_pool.
- Postmortem: include hedge consumption audit and customer impact timeline; recommend compensation when hedged experience still violated contracted SLAs.

UX and Customer Communication:
- In Console: dedicated "Hedge & Failback" tab for tenancy with clear status, graph of hedge balance, and CTA to replenish.
- Notifications: when hedge drops under 20% of starting balance -> automated email with options.
- Onboarding: default small hedge credit for all new Dedicated customers for first 30 days to smooth early adoption and reduce noisy failures.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- How big should default hedge allocations be? (cost vs utility tradeoff). Proposal: start with token equivalent to 2 hours of median usage at p95.
- Which model variants are acceptable for failback without breaking user experience? Need product/APIs to mark model variants with fallthrough quality tiers.
- Legal/billing: does absorbing delta in THC change contract terms (SLA credits vs billed hedging)? Need finance + legal check.
- Operational complexity: more routing paths increases debugging surface. Mitigation: strong structured telemetry + trace ids for cross-environment requests.

Risks:
- Customers may rely on hedges as permanent safety nets and under-provision core capacity, leading to sustained hidden cost transfers to hosted.
- Complexity in accurate attribution could cause disputes over billing when failback was opaque.
- Risk of oscillation if quiet-scale parameters mis-tuned (flip-flopping between Dedicated and fallback).

Next steps / proposed MVP roadmap:
1) Design spec (this doc) -> align with Product, Infra, SRE, Legal (2 weeks).
2) Small PoC: implement GFL routing flag + simple hosted fallback for a subset of tenants; basic hedge accounting (3 sprints).
3) Console + telemetry: show per-tenant hedging + failback traces (2 sprints).
4) Autoscaler integration and soft-decommit experiments (2 sprints).
5) Beta with 5–10 tenants, monitor, refine policies, and finalize pricing/legal (4–6 weeks).

Appendix: example failure scenario and flow
- Tenant A has high qps, reserved pool hits 94% util -> admission starts to queue. The autoscaler is mid-decision and cannot immediately add nodes (cold start). Route priority indicates critical requests for customer checkout route. Tenant A enrolled in THC with 80% balance. System routes 40% of critical checkout attempts to hosted fallback for 90s window, debiting THC. Traces include failback tag; Console surfaces spike. Autoscaler completes scale up in 120s; quiet-scale exponentially moves routing back over 30s. Tenant A spent 12% of hedge credits and receives an automated summary mail with token and cost delta.

Notes to reviewers:
- Focus review on: API ergonomics for tenants (are controls intuitive?), acceptable default hedge sizing, and failback model variant taxonomy.
- Please add comments in Confluence page linked above and tag @Priya Nair for product decisions and @Omar Suleiman for infra constraints.
